title: The TSbot bot may accept requests from every website
description: When a bot's allowedOrigins list is empty, the public API serves every origin. If TSbot's bot was never given an allow-list, any site can embed it and spend its daily quota from visitors' browsers.
claimed_root_cause: An empty allowedOrigins list means all origins are allowed (by design).

evidence.description: The setup step asks the owner to add the TSbot URL only if the list is not empty.

blockers: The bot's saved settings live in the production D1 and are not visible in the repository.

validation_plan.deployment: Hardened in code: PERMANENT_BOTS bots are now pinned to PERMANENT_BOT_ORIGINS (deploy.yml, default https://tsbot-nara.pages.dev), so an empty allow-list no longer opens TSbot to every site. After deploying, check that a request from another Origin to /api/public/info?bot=<TSbot id> gets 403. Scripts without an Origin header remain bounded only by the daily quotas.

title: XSS in the TSbot widget from AI answers or bot info

evidence.description: Text is escaped before any formatting; only fixed tags are added and numbers go through Number().

reason: Everything is escaped or set as textContent, themeColor is regex-checked, and the TSbot CSP has script-src 'self' without unsafe-inline.

title: Reflected CORS origin exposes private data
description: Origin is reflected when allowedOrigins is empty.

evidence.description: No Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header; the widget uses credentials: omit.

reason: Only public bot data is served and no credential travels, so there is no confidentiality impact.

title: Per-IP limits key on the full IPv6 address, so one host can rotate past them
description: Every per-IP control (sign-up 5 per day, sign-in lock 8 per 10 minutes, chat per-minute and daily per-visitor quotas) uses the raw cf-connecting-ip. A single IPv6 host normally owns a /64, so it gets a fresh bucket per address. That leaves only the global, per-bot and per-e-mail caps. One host can then use up the global sign-up cap (200 per day) and the bot's daily question cap, which affects TSbot, and can keep the platform admin locked out (100 failures per 10 minutes).
intended_behavior: A per-IP limit should bound one client, so IPv6 should be grouped by /64.

trace.description: allow() per-minute and dailyQuota per visitor.

evidence.description: The platform-admin global counter (100 per 10 minutes) refuses even the correct password once reached.
Global sign-up cap of 200 per day, shared by everyone.

conditions.description: The client reaches Cloudflare over IPv6 and Pseudo-IPv4 overwrite is off (the default).

instructions: In a local worker test, send sign-ups with cf-connecting-ip values from the same /64.
Count how many are accepted before the per-IP limit.
execution.observed_result: Before the fix, each address was a new bucket, so the per-IP limit never triggered. After the fix, clientKey() maps them all to 2001:db8:1:2::/64 (tests/unit/net.test.ts).

remediation.strategy: Group IPv6 addresses by /64 before keying limits: src/net.ts clientKey(), used by ip() in src/index.ts. IPv4 and IPv4-mapped addresses stay per address.

likelihood.reason: Most hosting and home connections give a /64.

impact.reason: Availability only: global caps still bound spend and no data is exposed.

confidence.reason: Source trace, confirmed by an independent verifier. The fix has unit tests, and the worker suite passes.

title: Permanent accounts are on by default, so an unverified e-mail can be claimed forever
description: Sign-up needs no e-mail verification. Earlier audits accepted that because an account expired after 7 days. The platform setting allowPermanent defaults to true, so anyone can register another person's e-mail as a permanent account. The real owner of that address can then never sign up, and nothing in the app can free the address except deleting the row by hand.
root_cause: getPlatform() treats a missing platform setting as allowPermanent=true, and sign-up and /api/auth/account give a never-expiring account to any anonymous caller who asks.
intended_behavior: An account whose e-mail was never verified must not hold that e-mail for good. Either it expires (7 days) or the address must be verified first.

trace.description: Anonymous sign-up with any e-mail and permanent:true.
allowPermanent: saved?.allowPermanent !== false, so true when never set.

evidence.description: An e-mail is freed for a new sign-up only when the old account has expired, which a permanent one never does.
The daily purge selects only expires_at <= now.
A 7-day account can also switch itself to permanent through /api/auth/account.
The sign-up checkbox #permanent is checked by default.
The test asserts the default policy is allowPermanent: true.

conditions.description: The platform admin has never turned off 'Izinkan pengguna memilih akun permanen' (the default).
The victim's e-mail is not registered yet.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous visitor of the Nara dashboard.
instructions: On a local wrangler dev instance with a fresh D1, sign up as victim@example.test with permanent:true.
Sign up again with the same e-mail from another client.
execution.observed_result: The first account gets expires_at 9999-12-31. The second sign-up is refused with 409 'already registered', and no cleanup ever frees the address. Source trace; the worker test suite exercises the same permanent path.

remediation.strategy: Fixed: getPlatform() now treats a missing setting as allowPermanent=false, so permanent accounts are an explicit opt-in by the platform admin (dashboard switch). Accounts that were already permanent stay permanent; turning the switch on and then off gives them 7 days (except PERMANENT_BOTS owners). A fuller fix would be e-mail verification for permanent accounts.

likelihood.reason: The attacker has to target a specific e-mail before its owner signs up.

impact.reason: The victim is permanently denied registration with their own address. No data or bot of the victim is exposed.

confidence.reason: Fully traced in source and confirmed by an independent verifier.

title: SSRF through a crafted Cloudflare Workers AI key
description: The account id from the key is placed in the URL.

trace.description: URL built from the key's account part.

evidence.description: The account must match ^[0-9a-f]{32}$; the host is fixed to api.cloudflare.com.

reason: Neither the host nor the path can be changed.
